title: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
summary: Why kernel I/O paths run out of cycles at line rate, and how DPDK and SPDK hand devices to user space with vfio-pci, hugepage DMA, poll-mode drivers, batched doorbells and per-core queues.
outcomes: Compute the per-packet and per-I/O cycle budget at a given link speed, clock and target rate
Explain how vfio-pci, BAR mapping, hugepages and the IOMMU let a process drive a device safely
Trace a poll-mode receive and transmit burst through descriptor rings, done flags and tail doorbells
Compute rte_ring occupancy across 32-bit wraparound and doorbell writes per I/O under batching
Decide between full bypass, bifurcated drivers, AF_XDP and the kernel stack for a given workload

lessons.title: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles

blocks.md:
Zero-copy I/O (the previous course) removed the data copies, but every packet or disk command still travels through the kernel: an interrupt, the kernel driver, generic bookkeeping structures, a system call to hand data to the program, and locks shared with every other user of the device.

**Kernel bypass** removes the kernel from that path entirely. The device driver runs *inside the application*: the program writes the device's registers itself and the device moves data straight into the program's memory by DMA (direct memory access, where the device reads and writes RAM without the CPU). DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit) does this for network cards, SPDK (Storage Performance Development Kit) for NVMe SSDs.

Why go that far? Count the time per packet. The smallest Ethernet frame is 64 bytes, and on the wire each frame also carries an 8 byte preamble and start delimiter plus a 12 byte gap before the next frame: 84 bytes, or 672 bits.

At 10 Gbit/s that is 10 x 10^9 / 672 = **14.88 million packets per second**, one packet every **67.2 ns**. The ixy paper (a teaching driver from the Technical University of Munich) benchmarks its forwarder and DPDK at exactly this load: 29.76 Mpps across two 10 Gbit/s ports.

blocks.caption: The whole budget for one core to receive, process and send one minimum-size packet at 10 Gbit/s line rate. The ixy paper rounds it to 200 cycles.

blocks.title: Cycle budget per packet versus link speed

curves.label: Budget at line rate, 64 B frames
Linux sk_buff alloc and free only

scenes.caption: At 3.0 GHz the budget is 2016 cycles at 1 Gbit/s but only 201.6 at 10 Gbit/s. ixy measured about 100 cycles per packet just to allocate and free Linux's packet struct (sk_buff) in Open vSwitch.
Read the curve at 100 Gbit/s: 20.2 cycles per packet. No single core keeps up there; the NIC spreads flows over several receive queues (receive side scaling), each polled by its own core.
At 2.4 GHz the 10 Gbit/s budget drops to 161.3 cycles. DPDK forwarded a packet in 61 cycles in ixy's test, which leaves room for real work.

blocks.md:
Storage hit the same wall once SSDs got fast. SPDK's developers set out to do 10 million 4 KiB reads per second on one core running at 4.0 GHz: 4.0 x 10^9 / 10^7 = **400 cycles (100 ns) per I/O**. In their benchmark a single division instruction, used to pick a random block address, already ate 6% of that budget.

At these budgets, fixed per-operation costs dominate: taking an interrupt, switching into the kernel, initializing a general-purpose metadata struct, grabbing a lock. Kernel bypass is a way to remove each of them.

blocks.title: Kernel path versus bypass path for one received packet

scenes.caption: The normal path: the NIC raises an interrupt, the kernel driver builds a packet struct, the stack processes it, and the program fetches it with a system call.
Each hop costs fixed cycles per packet no matter how small the packet is. Copies are only part of it.
Bypass: the NIC writes packets by DMA into buffers the application owns, and the application's own poll-mode driver (PMD) checks for them in a loop. No interrupt, no system call.
The kernel still has a small role: a stub driver (vfio-pci) hands the device to the process at startup. After that the data path never enters the kernel.

blocks.md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

blocks.prompt: A 25 Gbit/s port receives minimum-size frames and your core runs at 2.5 GHz. How many cycles does one core get per packet?
blocks.reveal: 672 bits / 25 Gbit/s = 26.88 ns per packet, times 2.5 GHz = **67.2 cycles**. That is about the cost of one L2 miss that hits L3 (roughly 20 ns, per SPDK's authors), and a single last-level cache miss to DRAM would blow the whole budget, so even a bypass driver needs several cores and several receive queues to reach line rate with real per-packet work.

blocks.question: Why do people benchmark packet I/O with 64 byte frames rather than 1500 byte frames?
options: Because they maximize packets per second, so fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, syscalls, metadata) dominate and are exposed
Because 64 byte frames are the most common size on real networks
Because NICs can only DMA 64 bytes at a time
Because larger frames do not fit in a 2 KiB packet buffer
blocks.explain: Throughput in bits is the same, but small frames mean the most packets per second, and most driver and stack costs are per packet, not per byte. That is the worst case a data plane must survive.

blocks.question: A design spends 100 cycles per packet allocating and initializing a generic packet struct. At 3.0 GHz, can one core forward 10 Gbit/s of minimum-size frames?
options: Yes, 100 cycles is well under the budget
Yes, as long as the copies are removed
No: the budget is about 200 cycles, and allocation alone takes half, leaving too little for receive, lookup and transmit
It depends only on the link's MTU
blocks.explain: The budget is 3.0 GHz x 67.2 ns, about 202 cycles. ixy measured DPDK's entire forwarding path at 61 cycles; a 100 cycle metadata step alone eats half of the line-rate budget before any real work.

lessons.title: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory

blocks.md: A driver needs three things from the hardware: its **registers**, which a PCIe device exposes as memory ranges called BARs (base address registers) so the CPU drives it with MMIO (memory-mapped I/O) loads and stores; **DMA memory** the device can read and write by address; and optionally **interrupts**. Normally only kernel code may touch any of these. Kernel bypass must hand all three to a process, safely.

Step one is taking the device away from its kernel driver. On Linux you *unbind* the device (a write to a file in sysfs) and *bind* it to `vfio-pci` (or the older `uio` drivers). SPDK's docs call these dummy drivers: they do not initialize the hardware, they just mark the device as taken so the kernel does not re-attach its real driver, and they expose it to user space.

Once unbound, the kernel cannot use the device: a port bound to vfio-pci is no longer a Linux network interface (and DPDK in turn ignores ports left under Linux control). For an NVMe SSD, `/dev/nvme0n1` disappears and any filesystem mounted on it goes with it: the whole kernel block stack is out of the picture.

blocks.code:
# load the VFIO driver and see who owns each port
sudo modprobe vfio-pci
./usertools/dpdk-devbind.py --status

# give port 82:00.0 to DPDK (it vanishes from Linux)
sudo ./usertools/dpdk-devbind.py --bind=vfio-pci 0000:82:00.0

# reserve 1024 x 2 MB hugepages (2 GiB) for packet buffers
echo 1024 | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages

# later: hand the port back to the kernel ixgbe driver
sudo ./usertools/dpdk-devbind.py --bind=ixgbe 0000:82:00.0
blocks.caption: Commands from DPDK's Linux getting-started guide. Binding needs root; viewing status does not.

blocks.title: How a process takes ownership of a device through VFIO

scenes.caption: At boot the kernel's own driver owns the NIC and Linux uses it as a normal network interface.
dpdk-devbind unbinds ixgbe and binds vfio-pci. vfio-pci does not program the NIC; it only claims it and exposes it under /dev/vfio.
The process opens the VFIO device and maps the device's BAR into its address space. Writing to that memory is now a register write on the NIC.
The process registers its hugepage buffers with the IOMMU (VFIO_IOMMU_MAP_DMA). The device gets I/O virtual addresses (IOVAs) that the IOMMU translates and checks.
Steady state: the device DMAs packets through the IOMMU into the buffers and the process drives registers directly. The kernel is not on the data path.

blocks.md:
Now the hard part: DMA. A device does not understand the process's virtual addresses. Without an IOMMU it needs **physical** addresses, and Linux gives no guarantee that a virtual page keeps the same physical page: swapping, compaction and memory hot-add can all move it. `mlock` only prevents swapping; POSIX has no call that pins a physical address.

DPDK and SPDK solve this with **hugepages** (2 MiB by default). Linux does not move them today, they are physically contiguous inside each page, and fewer pages also means fewer TLB misses. That is why SPDK insists that I/O buffers come from `spdk_dma_malloc()` and friends.

blocks.title: Why a moved page breaks DMA, and how the IOMMU fixes it

scenes.caption: A buffer of four ordinary 4 KiB pages. The driver looked up their physical frames (for example in /proc/self/pagemap) and gave those addresses to the device.
Simplified: the kernel compacts memory and moves v1 to frame p311. The device still holds p903, so its next DMA writes into memory that now belongs to someone else.
Hugepages: the same buffer lives inside one 2 MiB page, physically contiguous and never moved by Linux today, so one lookup stays valid.
With an IOMMU the device is given I/O virtual addresses. VFIO maps each IOVA to the buffer's pages and keeps them in place, and a stray DMA outside the mappings is blocked.

blocks.md: The IOMMU (I/O memory management unit) is what makes VFIO safe. VFIO grants devices by **IOMMU group**, the smallest set of devices the hardware can isolate from everything else. A device behind a PCIe-to-PCI bridge shares a group with the bridge, so all of them must be given to VFIO (or left without a driver) together.

No IOMMU, no safety. `uio_pci_generic`, `igb_uio` and VFIO's `enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode` let the device DMA to any physical address. A bug in the application then corrupts the kernel or other processes: the ixy authors report losing a filesystem to rogue DMA writes on a misconfigured server. DPDK recommends vfio-pci with the IOMMU enabled.

blocks.question: You bind the NVMe SSD that holds a mounted /data filesystem to vfio-pci so an SPDK app can use it. What happens to /data?
options: It keeps working; SPDK and the kernel share the drive
The kernel loses the device: /dev/nvme0n1 disappears and the filesystem on it is gone from the kernel's view
It becomes read-only until SPDK exits
SPDK mounts it in user space automatically
blocks.explain: Unbinding removes the kernel driver, so the block device and everything built on it vanish. SPDK provides its own user-space storage layers, but not the kernel filesystem you had mounted.

blocks.question: Why do DPDK and SPDK allocate I/O buffers from hugepages rather than plain malloc memory?
options: Because NICs cannot DMA into 4 KiB pages
Because VFIO only accepts 1 GiB pages
Because hugepages are faster for the device to read over PCIe
Because hugepages have physical addresses that Linux does not move today and are contiguous within a page, and they also cut TLB misses
blocks.explain: The device must be given addresses that stay valid. Hugepages are not migrated by Linux today and each one is physically contiguous; the TLB benefit is a bonus. With an IOMMU, VFIO pins and maps them explicitly.

lessons.title: Poll-mode drivers: descriptor rings, doorbells and bursts

blocks.md:
Recall from NVMe that a device and its driver share **rings** in host memory. A NIC works the same way. A receive (RX) ring is an array of small descriptors, 16 bytes each on the Intel 82599 that ixy drives. At startup the driver fills every descriptor with the physical address of an empty packet buffer from a **memory pool** (mempool) of fixed-size buffers.

Ownership passes between NIC and driver through two indexes: the NIC advances a **head** as it fills buffers, and the driver advances a **tail** register to give descriptors back.

When a packet arrives the NIC DMAs it into the next buffer and sets a *done* flag in that descriptor. The driver can detect this in two ways. Reading the NIC's head register costs a PCIe round trip. Reading the done flag costs almost nothing, because the device's DMA write lands in the CPU's last-level cache: ixy describes it as the difference between a cache miss and a cache hit for every packet. So poll-mode drivers check flags in memory, and only *write* the tail register, once per batch.

blocks.title: One receive queue through a burst (8 descriptors)

scenes.caption: Simplified 8-slot ring. Every descriptor points at an empty buffer and belongs to the NIC. The driver's next slot to check is 0.
Three packets arrive. The NIC DMAs them into the buffers of slots 0 to 2 and sets each done flag. No interrupt is raised; nobody is told.
rte_eth_rx_burst() reads the flags in slots 0, 1, 2 (cache hits), returns the 3 buffers to the app, and stops at slot 3, which is not done.
The driver puts 3 fresh mempool buffers into slots 0 to 2, then does one MMIO write of the tail register to hand all 3 back. One doorbell for the whole burst.
The next poll finds slot 3 not done and returns 0 packets at once: no blocking, no register access. The loop simply polls again.

blocks.md: The application side is a loop that never sleeps. Below is the core of DPDK's [l2fwd example](https://github.com/DPDK/dpdk/blob/main/examples/l2fwd/main.c), lightly trimmed. Each worker core (an *lcore*, a thread DPDK pins to one CPU) polls its port for up to 32 packets, rewrites the MAC addresses, and queues them for transmit.

blocks.title: The l2fwd main loop, one iteration at a time

scenes.caption: Idle link. rx_burst returns 0 and the loop spins straight back. The core shows 100% busy even though no work is done.
A burst arrives: rx_burst returns 32 packet pointers (mbufs) in one call, the maximum the loop asked for.
Each packet is rewritten in place and added to a transmit buffer. When the buffer reaches 32 packets it is sent as one TX burst with one tail-register write.
Only 5 packets trickle in. They sit in the TX buffer until the timer check, about every 100 us, flushes them so a slow trickle is not delayed forever.

blocks.prompt: Interrupts let a core sleep until a packet arrives. At a light load of 0.1 Mpps, would you expect interrupt-driven receive to have lower or higher latency than busy polling?
blocks.reveal: **Higher.** ixy measured median forwarding latency of 3.8 us with polling versus 7.7 us with interrupts (no throttling), 11.3 us with 10 us interrupt throttling and 107.4 us with 200 us throttling. An interrupt must wake the CPU from a sleep state, switch into interrupt context and then still poll the NIC. Polling skips all of that, paid for in power.

blocks.title: Forwarding latency at 0.1 Mpps: polling versus interrupts (ixy)

scenes.caption: Median latency. Interrupt throttling (ITR, a minimum gap between interrupts) makes the NIC wait before signalling, adding delay directly.
99.99th percentile. Tails grow too: 5.8 us polling against 11.0 and 15.3 us with interrupts and 240 us with heavy throttling.
Maximum observed. Polling stays at 15.8 us; interrupts reach 76.6 and 78.4 us. Measured on one ixy test system with hardware timestamps.

blocks.md: Bursts matter for the same reason. Every receive or transmit ends in an MMIO write of a tail register, which ixy calls a slow operation, so both ixy and DPDK update it once per batch. DPDK's vector (SIMD) transmit path even requires bursts of at least 4. Gains flatten out, though: ixy saw L1 cache misses per packet rise as batches grew, and recommends not making batches too large.

blocks.title: Simplified model: throughput per core versus burst size

scenes.caption: Simplified model, not a measurement: a per-burst cost d (doorbell write, function call) is shared by B packets. With an assumed d of 300 cycles, B = 1 gives 6.7 Mpps.
At B = 32 the per-burst cost is under 10 cycles per packet and the curve is nearly flat. Beyond that, real systems also pay L1 cache misses the model ignores.
At 1.2 GHz no burst size reaches line rate: per-packet work, not the doorbell, is now the limit. ixy saw the same flattening at 1.2 GHz.

blocks.question: A new driver checks for received packets by reading the NIC's head register on every poll. What is the main problem?
options: Each read is a PCIe round trip, while the done flag in the descriptor is already in the CPU cache
Nothing; it is the standard method
Reading the head register disables DMA
The head register is only valid after an interrupt
blocks.explain: MMIO reads stall the core for a full trip across PCIe. Checking the done flag written by DMA into the last-level cache is far cheaper; drivers only write the tail register, once per burst.

blocks.question: Your forwarder calls rte_eth_tx_burst with one packet at a time and throughput is poor. Which change helps most?
options: Increase the RX ring from 1024 to 8192 descriptors
Switch the port to interrupt mode
Collect packets and transmit them in bursts of around 32, so one tail write covers many packets
Allocate packet buffers with malloc instead of a mempool
blocks.explain: Per-call and per-doorbell costs are fixed, so sharing them across a burst divides them by the burst size. Larger rings do not add throughput (ixy found none above 64 descriptors) and interrupts add latency.

lessons.title: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools

blocks.md:
One core cannot do 100 Gbit/s, so a bypass application must scale across cores, and at a budget of tens of cycles even an uncontended atomic instruction hurts. The rule in both projects is the same: **give each core its own hardware queue and never share it**.

DPDK's poll-mode driver guide: each receive queue is polled by a single lcore, each core gets its own transmit queue per port, and sharing queues between cores "requires global locks and severely impacts performance". SPDK: a queue pair has no locks or atomics, so only one thread may use it at a time, and the driver does not check this, because checking would need a lock.

Why can a user-space driver do this when the kernel cannot? An application knows exactly how many threads it created. A kernel driver serves every process on the machine with a thread population that changes all the time, so it maps hardware queues to CPU cores and takes a lock to coordinate the threads that run on each core. SPDK's authors call the difference "very minor, but measurable" for NVMe. Most NVMe drives offer 32 to 128 queue pairs, enough for one per thread.

scenes.caption: Run-to-completion: the NIC hashes each flow to one receive queue. lcore 0 owns queue 0, lcore 1 owns queue 1; each receives, processes and transmits its own packets with no shared state.
Pipeline: lcore 1 only receives, then passes packet pointers to a worker core through a lockless ring. Useful when processing is heavy or staged.
What is never allowed: two lcores polling one queue. That needs a lock around every burst, the exact cost bypass was meant to remove.

blocks.md:
Cores that must talk use **rte_ring**, DPDK's fixed-size lockless FIFO of pointers. It keeps a producer head and tail and a consumer head and tail. A producer reserves slots by moving the producer head (one 32-bit compare-and-swap when several producers race), copies its pointers in, then publishes them by moving the producer tail. Consumers do the mirror image. Because whole bursts are reserved in one step, dequeuing 32 objects costs about the same as dequeuing one.

The indexes are free-running unsigned 32-bit counters that are never reset; the slot is the index masked by size - 1 (size is a power of two).

blocks.caption: Unsigned subtraction wraps automatically, so the formulas stay correct when a counter overflows. The ring always keeps between 0 and size - 1 entries.

scenes.caption: Empty ring, mask 7. Both counters equal 4294967294 (2^32 - 2), which masks to slot 6. entries = 0, free = 7: one slot always stays empty.
Enqueue a burst of 4: slots 6, 7, 0, 1. prod becomes 4294967294 + 4, which wraps to 2. entries = (2 - 4294967294) mod 2^32 = 4; free = 3.
Dequeue a burst of 3 (pkt1, pkt2, pkt3). cons becomes 1. entries = 2 - 1 = 1; free = 7 + 1 - 2 = 6. No counter was ever reset.

blocks.md:
Packet buffers come from a **mempool**, whose free list is itself a ring. Hitting that shared ring for every buffer would mean a compare-and-swap per packet, so each core keeps a small private **cache** (a stack of free pointers) and only moves buffers to or from the shared ring in bulk.

The cost is idle buffers parked in caches, which you must size for. l2fwd creates its pool with `max(ports x (rx_desc + tx_desc + burst + lcores x cache), 8192)`. With 2 ports, 1024 RX and TX descriptors, a burst of 32, one lcore and a 256-entry cache that is max(4672, 8192) = 8192 buffers.

SPDK pushes the same idea up the whole stack ([message passing and concurrency](https://spdk.io/doc/concurrency.html)). Shared data is owned by one thread; other threads send it a message, a function pointer plus a context pointer, through a lockless ring, and the owner runs it. Lightweight `spdk_thread`s and `spdk_poller`s (functions called repeatedly by a thread) replace blocking calls.

Scaling rule for bypass stacks: **one queue, one owner**. Hardware queues give each core a private path to the device, mempool caches give it private buffers, and rings or messages are the only places cores meet, always in bursts.

blocks.question: To balance load, a developer lets two threads submit I/O to the same SPDK NVMe queue pair. What happens?
options: SPDK detects it and adds a lock automatically
It works, but throughput halves
The second thread's submissions are rejected with an error
Undefined behavior: queue pairs have no locks or atomics, and SPDK does not enforce single-thread use
blocks.explain: SPDK's NVMe docs state that violating the one-thread-per-queue-pair rule is undefined behavior and is not checked, because checking would itself need a lock. Give each thread its own queue pair instead.

blocks.question: An rte_ring of size 16 has prod_tail = 3 and cons_head = 4294967295. How many entries does it hold?
options: It is corrupted: prod is behind cons
blocks.explain: (3 - 4294967295) mod 2^32 = 4. The producer counter simply wrapped past 2^32 - 1; unsigned 32-bit subtraction gives the right distance without any special case.

blocks.question: Why does each lcore get its own mempool cache instead of every core taking buffers straight from the pool's shared ring?
options: To avoid a compare-and-swap on a shared, contended structure for every buffer; the cache refills in bulk
Because the shared ring can only be used by one core
Because caches are stored in the NIC
To make buffers physically contiguous
blocks.explain: Every access to the shared ring is an atomic operation on a cache line that all cores fight over. A private cache turns that into a plain array access, touching the shared ring only once per bulk refill or flush.

lessons.title: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread

blocks.md:
Recall from NVMe internals: the host writes 64 byte commands into a **submission queue** (SQ) in memory, rings a **doorbell** register to say how far it has written, and the drive writes 16 byte results into a **completion queue** (CQ), flipping a *phase bit* in each new entry so the host can tell new from old.

SPDK's NVMe driver is a C library that maps the drive's BAR into the process and follows the NVMe specification itself. It spawns no threads. `spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read()` builds a command in the SQ and returns at once; the app later calls `spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions()`, which scans the CQ for flipped phase bits and runs your callback for each finished command.

blocks.title: Three reads on one queue pair with batched doorbells

scenes.caption: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell queue-pair option on, the app submits 3 reads. Each call only writes a 64 byte command into the SQ in memory. Nothing has crossed PCIe yet.
One MMIO write to the SQ tail doorbell tells the drive about all 3 commands. MMIO writes are posted: the core does not wait for an answer.
The drive fetches the commands by DMA, DMAs the data straight into the app's pinned buffers (zero copy), and writes 3 completion entries with the new phase bit.
The app's poll reads CQ memory, sees 3 flipped phase bits, and runs 3 callbacks. No interrupt was involved.
One MMIO write of the CQ head doorbell releases all 3 entries. Total: 2 doorbell writes for 3 I/Os instead of 6.

blocks.md:
Why count doorbells? SPDK's authors explain that MMIO writes queue up inside the CPU before going out over PCIe, and if that queue overflows the core stalls. A driver that rings a doorbell for every submission and every completion would be **capped below about 4 million I/O per second on most platforms**.

SPDK attacks both sides. Completion: like most NVMe drivers, it rings the CQ head doorbell once per poll call, not once per entry. Submission: an optional queue-pair setting defers the SQ doorbell until the next poll call, so every command submitted since the last poll shares one doorbell.

blocks.caption: B = commands submitted per SQ doorbell, C = completions reaped per CQ doorbell. Simplified: SPDK can delay the CQ doorbell even longer, until the drive is about to run out of CQ slots.

blocks.title: Doorbell writes per I/O, and what batching bought SPDK

scenes.caption: From the formula: 2 MMIO writes per I/O with no batching, 1.125 and 1.031 with submit batching only, and 0.056 when each poll also reaps about 40 completions (SPDK saw 30 to 50 per poll under load).
Per million I/Os that is 2,000,000 versus 56,250 doorbell writes, a 35.6x reduction. Measured on SPDK's test system: 2.89M IOPS without deferred submit doorbells versus 10.39M with them.

blocks.md:
Now the budget. The test CPU (a Xeon Platinum 8280L) ran at 4.0 GHz turbo, so 10 million I/Os per second leaves **400 cycles per I/O**. Waiting on main memory even a few times per I/O would blow that, so the rest of the work is cache discipline:

- The driver touches about 5 cache lines per I/O. With 21 SSDs at queue depth 128 that is 128 x 5 x 21 = 13,440 lines, or 840 KiB of hot data.
- Structures are rearranged (checked with the `pahole` tool) so hot-path fields share cache lines and error-path fields move elsewhere, and submission-path and completion-path fields are kept on separate lines.
- Link-time optimization was on; the CPU used one thread on one core.

blocks.prompt: The benchmark kept 21 SSDs at queue depth 128 busy and completed 10.39 million I/Os per second. Using Little's law (in-flight = rate x time), what was the average time each I/O spent outstanding?
blocks.reveal: In flight: 21 x 128 = 2,688 I/Os. Time = 2,688 / 10.39 x 10^6 per s = **259 us** (derived here; SPDK's post does not report it). One core spends only about 100 ns of CPU per I/O; the rest of each I/O's life is the drives working. That is the point: the CPU cost per I/O, not device latency, was the bottleneck being removed.

blocks.md: You rarely need many queue pairs per drive. SPDK's docs note that the full performance of a device is almost always reachable with one queue pair: 4 queue pairs at depth 32 behave like 1 at depth 128. Add queue pairs to add threads, not to add speed.

Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` tool than using fio with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

blocks.question: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell option on, a thread calls spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read 16 times and then calls spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions once. How many SQ tail doorbell writes did those 16 submissions need?
options: 0, NVMe needs no doorbell
blocks.explain: With the option set, submission only builds commands in the SQ ring; the doorbell is rung inside the poll call, once for everything submitted since the last poll.

blocks.question: Why does SPDK complete I/O by polling instead of waiting for interrupts?
options: NVMe drives cannot generate interrupts
With an I/O finishing every microsecond or less, taking an interrupt (stop, switch stacks, pollute the cache) costs too much, and routing interrupts to a user process is impractical
Polling uses less power
Interrupts are only available to the kernel's io_uring
blocks.explain: SPDK's docs give both reasons: interrupts into user space are not feasible for most hardware designs, and interrupt handling adds jitter and forced context switches. When completions arrive constantly, checking CQ memory is cheaper.

lessons.title: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else

blocks.md:
Bypass is not free. The bill comes in four parts:

1. **Burned cores.** A poll loop shows 100% CPU even with no traffic. DPDK's power library can back off after a run of empty polls (pause), sleep until the RX descriptor's memory changes (monitor, on CPUs with the WAITPKG instructions), or scale core frequency with load. Some PMDs also support interrupt mode, but this is per-driver.
2. **No kernel services.** A bound port has no kernel TCP/IP stack, and tools like ethtool and tcpdump cannot see it. An SPDK drive has no kernel filesystem; SPDK supplies its own user-space block layers.
3. **Safety depends on the IOMMU.** Without one, the application can DMA over anything.
4. **Tuning traps.** Dedicated cores, hugepage reservations, NUMA-local memory, and buffer counts all become your job.

blocks.prompt: A common tuning tip says to raise RX and TX rings to 4096 or 8192 descriptors for more throughput. What did ixy measure when its forwarder was overloaded at 29 Mpps?
blocks.reveal: No throughput gain above 64 descriptors, and **latency that grows linearly with ring size**: median 8.3 us with 64-entry rings, 50.9 us with 512 and 424.7 us with 4096. A full ring is just a queue: every packet waits behind every buffered packet. Under a non-overloaded 15 Mpps load the ring size barely mattered (5.2 to 5.4 us).

blocks.title: Median forwarding latency by ring size (ixy)

scenes.caption: At 15 Mpps the forwarder keeps up, rings stay nearly empty, and ring size makes almost no difference.
At 29 Mpps the forwarder is overloaded and packets are dropped. Rings fill up, and latency scales with how much they hold.

blocks.md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

There are middle grounds that keep the kernel in charge of the device:

- **Bifurcated driver** (for example NVIDIA ConnectX): the kernel driver keeps controlling the NIC while the DPDK PMD runs the data path, and NIC flow rules decide which traffic goes to DPDK and which to the kernel. ethtool and normal interfaces keep working ([flow bifurcation](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/howto/flow_bifurcation.html)).
- **AF_XDP**: an XDP program in the kernel driver redirects frames into a user-space memory area (UMEM) via shared rings ([AF_XDP docs](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/af_xdp.html)). The NIC stays under its kernel driver and remains a Linux device.
- **io_uring** for storage and sockets: shared rings and batching, with the kernel's filesystems and stack intact.

blocks.title: Who keeps the device: a spectrum of options

scenes.caption: Left to right: more raw packet rate, less kernel. The kernel stack gives every tool and protocol; full bypass gives the most packets per cycle and nothing else.
Need line rate on minimum-size packets with dedicated cores and your own protocol code? Full bypass.
Need SSH and monitoring on the same port as a fast data plane? A bifurcated driver splits traffic in NIC hardware.
Moderate rates, normal TCP, shared machine? Stay in the kernel; io_uring already batches system calls away.

blocks.md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

blocks.question: A firewall appliance must filter 40 Mpps of mostly small packets, but operators also need SSH and normal monitoring on the same 100 Gbit/s port. Which design fits best?
options: Kernel stack with larger socket buffers
Full vfio-pci bypass and a hand-written SSH server inside the DPDK app
Interrupt-mode DPDK with 8192-entry rings
A bifurcated driver (or flow bifurcation) so the data plane runs in DPDK and control traffic stays with the kernel
blocks.explain: Flow bifurcation lets NIC hardware steer data-plane flows to the PMD and the rest to Linux, keeping kernel tools. Full bypass would remove the kernel's view of the port; huge rings only add latency.

blocks.question: A key-value service handles 50,000 requests per second per machine, shares cores with other services, and runs on laptops for development. Should it adopt DPDK?
options: Probably not: per-request kernel overhead is a tiny part of its budget, and bypass would burn dedicated cores, need root-level device setup and lose kernel tooling
Yes, bypass always lowers latency
Yes, but only with UIO to avoid needing an IOMMU
Yes, because hugepages alone will double its throughput
blocks.explain: At 50k requests per second each request has about 20 us of one core, so saving a microsecond of kernel path is noise. Bypass pays off near line rate, not for ordinary services.
